body.p: Claims 2-20 are pending in the present application, of which claim 2 is an
independent claim. Claims 3 and 6 have been amended herein for clarification. No new
matter is provided by the amendments made herein.
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement filed 9/21/2021 failed to comply with 37 CPR

1.98(a)(3)(i) because it did not include a concise explanation of the relevance, as it is presently understood by the individual designated in 37 CPR 1.56(c) most knowledgeable about the content of the information, of each reference listed that is not in the English language. A copy of the cited non-patent literature document including an English
translation is enclosed in an Information Disclosure Statement (cite no. 1) filed herewith.
Claim 2 has been interpreted under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
Claims 2-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph as being
indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which
the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The Office Action appears to assert that that the disclosure is devoid of any

structure that performs the function of "robotic assembly" in the claim. The Applicants respectfully disagree. The specification as filed, at least at paragraph [00151] and FIG. 6, clearly links the function of the "robotic assembly" to a claimed structure. Paragraph
[00151] is reproduced as follows, with emphasis:
System 10 can include robotic control assembly 850, such as a robot or
other assembly configured to control one or more linkages, cables or other
robotic control mechanisms. Robotic control assembly 850 includes control conduit 859 which can be operably attached to one or more
robotically manipulatable assemblies of system 10. As shown in FIG. 6,
control conduit can be operably attached to one or more of: diagnostic
catheter 100 via cable 851 ablation catheter 200 via cable 852; second diagnostic catheter 500 via cable 853; second ablation catheter 600 via
cable 854; and catheter device 700 via cable 855. Each catheter device
of system 10 can include one or more robotically manipulatable
assemblies such as a steering mechanism and/or a catheter shaft
advancing and/or retracting mechanism. In some embodiments, robotic
control assembly 850 is used to steer, advance and/or retract diagnostic
catheter 100 and/or ablation catheter 200. Robotic control assembly 850
can be used to manually (e.g. operator driven), semi-automatically (e.g.
operator driven and system 10 driven) or automatically (e.g. fully driven
by system 10) navigate one or more catheter devices of system 10.
System 10 can be configured to receive operator (e.g. clinician) input
information, such as clinician input information used to semi- automatically or automatically navigate one or more catheter devices of
system 10.
It would be clear to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was
made that the written description discloses the corresponding structure for performing the
entire claimed invention and clearly links the structure to the function.
In addition, claims 3 and 6 has been amended herein for clarification.
Reconsideration and removal of the rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112, second
paragraph are respectfully requested.
35 U.S.C. 103 Rejections
Claims 2-10 and 13-18 were rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being
unpatentable over Willis et al. (U.S. Patent No. 6,216,027) in view of Foley et al. (U.S.
Publication 2011/0028894).
It is submitted that Willis and Foley, alone or in combination, fail to teach or
suggest at least:
2. A catheter system comprising:
a diagnostic catheter comprising:

an elongate shaft comprising a distal end; an expandable assembly mounted to the elongate shaft, the expandable assembly comprising multiple splines and configured to transition from a compacted state to an expanded state;
a plurality of electrodes coupled to the multiple splines of the expandable assembly, each electrode configured to receive electrical signals;

a plurality of ultrasound transducers coupled to the multiple splines of the expandable assembly; and a steerable portion configured to be robotically manipulated; an ablation catheter comprising: an elongate shaft comprising a distal portion; at least one ablation element positioned on the ablation catheter shaft distal portion and configured to deliver energy to tissue; and
a steerable portion configured to be robotically manipulated;

a distance measurement assembly configured to drive the plurality of ultrasound transducers to produce anatomical geometry data, and to generate data representing a distance between each ultrasound transducer of the plurality of ultrasound transducers and a tissue surface orthogonal to each ultrasound transducer; a processing unit configured to create a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the produced anatomical geometry data, create electrical information based on the received electric signals, and display the electrical information in relation to the three-dimensional anatomical map; and

a robotic assembly configured to manipulate the steerable portion of the diagnostic catheter and/or steerable portion of the ablation catheter based on the anatomical geometry data produced by the distance measurement assembly.
Willis appears to disclose a device localization system that uses ultrasound

reference catheter(s) to establish a fixed 3D coordinate system within a heart using time- of-flight triangulation of ultrasound signals to determine the relative positions of ultrasound transducers on the reference and other catheters. The 3D coordinate system is represented graphically on a video monitor and is used to show the relative position and orientation of devices and to represent activity measured by mapping electrodes, ablation devices, and/or
certain anatomic structures.

During use of the system of the invention, one or more of the reference catheters 10 is introduced into the heart or the surrounding vasculature (or even into other areas such as the esophagus) and is left in place for the

duration of the procedure. Once reference catheter(s) 10 are positioned within or near a patient's heart, the system first measures the distances between each of the reference catheter transducers using the "time of flight" principal. It then uses these distances to establish the relative positions of the reference transducers and therefore to establish a three-dimensional coordinate system. [Willis, column 5, lines 55-65]

The reference catheter(s) 10 thereby establish an internal coordinate system by which the relative positions of EP catheter transducers in the heart may be calculated using triangulation and shown in real-time on a three dimensional display. [Willis, column 6, lines 52-56]
A marking catheter is employed to identify the location of anatomical landmarks
relative to the 3D coordinate system, not to create a three-dimensional anatomical map
based on the produced anatomical geometry data.

Referring to Fig. 9, the system of the present invention preferably utilizes a catheter 1 2 to identify the locations of anatomical landmarks (such as the septal wall) relative to the coordinate system so that the landmarks may be included on the three-dimensional display. Showing anatomical landmarks on the display correlates the three-dimensional coordinate system to discrete anatomical locations and thereby assists the physician in navigating EP catheters to the desired locations within the heart. [Willis, column 9, lines 3- 11, emphasis added]
Willis employs the coordinate system of a basket catheter to guide an ablation
catheter to a location corresponding to a location of a basket electrode.

For example, data corresponding to electrode locations on a mapping basket 14 may be saved in the system memory, together with data representing EP measurements taken by EP electrodes corresponding to the transducer locations. If, after the mapping basket 14 has been removed from the patient, the user wishes to guide an ablation catheter to a location corresponding to one of the basket electrodes, s/he may elect to display the saved location information for the basket simultaneously with the real time position of the ablation catheter. The graphical user interface is further provided with several additional functions that improve the accuracy and usefulness of the system. [Willis, column 17, lines 55-64]
Willis uses time of flight and triangulation to measure distances among ultrasound
transducers. Willis in no way teaches, suggests or discloses generating data representing a
distance between each ultrasound transducer of the plurality of ultrasound transducers and
a tissue surface orthogonal to each ultrasound transducer, as claimed.

These distance values are then used by the triangulation processor 126 (Fig. 1) to determine the relative positions of the ultrasound transducers, and the microprocessor 112 uses the position data to create a three-dimensional display of the catheters. [Willis, column 17, lines 35-39] As noted above, Willis teaches the creation of a coordinate system, but the

coordinate system is a catheter-centered coordinate system and Willis does not create a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the produced anatomical geometry data, but rather of a catheter. Additionally, Willis does not determine the distance between each ultrasound transducer and a tissue surface orthogonal thereto, and, as a result, is incapable of creating a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the produced anatomical geometry data. Willis discloses determining distances between transducers, not
between transducers and a tissue surface.
As the Office Action merely relies on Foley for disclosing the use of a robotic
device to steer a catheter/medical device in the body of a patient, Applicants respectfully submit that Foley fails to supply the requisite teaching, suggestion or disclosure to
overcome the deficiencies as described above with regard to Willis.
Accordingly, since Willis and Foley fail to teach or suggest these claimed features,

there is no way to combine the references to obtain teaching or suggestion of the claimed features. Further, the differences between the combination of Willis and Foley, and the present invention as claimed would not have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the
art at the time the invention was made.
Since Willis and Foley, taken alone or in combination, fail to teach, suggest or
disclose the present inventions set forth in claim 2, claim 2 and all claims dependent thereon, are believed to be allowable over the combination of the cited references.
Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections of claim 2 and all claims
dependent thereon under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on Willis and Foley is respectfully
requested.

Claim 20 was rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over
Willis in view of Foley as applied above, and further in view of Zanelli et al. (U.S. Patent
Zanelli appears to show an ultrasound device for transmyocardial revascularization:
the creation of channels in the myocardium. To effect the creation of channels, Zanelli employs an ultrasound ranging device to determine the distance between the tip of a
treatment tool and a surface of cardiovascular tissue.

The system also comprises a signal interface extending from the ultrasound transducer and signal processing component operatively connected to the signal interface for real time determination of at least one boundary surface of cardiovascular tissue relative to one or more positions of the distal tip of the treatment tool. A method of delivering laser energy to tissue is disclosed, the method including the steps of positioning the firing tip of a laser delivery means adjacent the front surface of the tissue, delivering laser energy to the tissue, transmitting ultrasound energy to the tissue, receiving ultrasound signals reflected from at least the rear surface of the tissue, and determining the distance between the firing tip of the laser delivery means and the rear surface of the tissue. [Abstract]
Zanelli merely teaches the use of an ultrasound transducer to measure the distance

from a distal tip of a treatment tool and a surface of cardiovascular tissue. Zanelli employs the distance, not to produce anatomical geometry data, nor to proceed from there to use that anatomical geometry data to create a three-dimensional anatomical map, but simply to
ensure that channels are created to a proper depth.
Neither Willis nor Zanelli teach or suggest, at least, a set of multidimensional

anatomical geometry data representing a distance between each ultrasound transducer and a tissue surface orthogonal to each ultrasound transducer, nor do they teach or suggest a processing unit configured to create a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the
produced anatomical geometry data.
Zanelli fails to supply the requisite teaching, suggestion or disclosure to overcome
the deficiencies as described above with regard to Willis and Foley.
Accordingly, since Willis, Foley and Zanelli fail to teach or suggest these claimed

features, there is no way to combine the references to obtain teaching or suggestion of the claimed features. Further, the differences between the combination of Willis, Foley and Zanelli, and the present invention as claimed would not have been obvious to one of
ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
Since Willis, Foley and Zanelli, taken alone or in combination, fail to teach, suggest
or disclose the present inventions set forth in claim 2, claim 2 and all claims dependent thereon, are believed to be allowable over the combination of the cited references.
Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections of claim 20 and all claims dependent thereon under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on Willis, Foley and Zanelli is
respectfully requested.
